L544@P9: The sizes of Kot Diji Phase mud bricks at Harappa
L545@P9: are very similar to those made during the Ravi Phase,
L546@P9: but they were much more unirorm because they were
L547@P9: mould made. Mud brick was used to build domestic
L548@P9: structures as well as to construct platforms and city
L549@P9: walls. Large mud bricks, measuring 10 x 20 x 40 cm,

L560@P9: The large-size mud bricks, 10 x 20 x 40 cm, were
L561@P9: occasionally used for house foundations or platforms,

L567@P9: Because of the limited exposure of Kot Diji Phase
L568@P9: occupations at Harappa, it is not possible to get a full
L569@P9: layout of houses, but they were generally oriented with
L570@P9: the cardinal directions and situated along wide unpaved
L571@P9: streets. On Mound AB, the north-south street measures approximately 5 meters wide. The house walls
L572@P9: range in width from 7 em, which is the width of one
L573@P9: mud brick, to more than 1 meter wide lOr fuundation or
L574@P9: platrorm walls.
L575@P9: The long continuity in building orientation and
L576@P9: brick sizes, from the Ravi through the Kot Diji Phase
L577@P9: occupations, cannot be coincidental and must be linked
L578@P9: to deeply held socioreligious beliefs associated with
L579@P9: settlement organization. The orientation of houses
L580@P9: according to the cardinal directions can be done using
L581@P9: the morning and afternoon shadows cast by a stick
L582@P9: placed in the center of a circle. More complex methods
L583@P9: involve sighting on the stars or eonstellations that rise
L584@P9: in the east or set in the west, The ~north star' at around
L585@P9: 2300 BCE was a very dim star called Draconis, and it
L586@P9: is unlikely that it was used for sighting during the prehistoric period (Parpola 1994). Astronomers calculate
L587@P9: that the Pleiades would have arisen in approximately
L588@P9: this same spot during each vernal equinox from 2720
L589@P9: to 1760 BCE, and this may have been the constellation used lOr orientating Early Harappan as well as
L590@P9: Harappan buildings (ibid.).
L591@P9: Geometric button seals
L592@P9: While it is possible to speculate about the cosmological
L593@P9: significance ofbuilding orientation and street layout, the
L594@P9: discovery ofgeometric designs carved on bone or steatite
L595@P9: button seals provides a more direct indication ofspecific
L596@P9: ideologies related to space and organization. The earliest
L597@P9: carved bone se.l from the Ravi Phase is fragmentary but
L598@P9: appears to represent one arm of the swastika motif that
L599@P9: becomes widespread during the later Harappan Period.
L600@P9: The swastika diagram can be interpreted as an effort to
L601@P9: create order out of chaos. By dividing chaos into four
L602@P9: quarters and turning it in the right direction, order, balance .nd progress are achieved. In later Hindu iconography, the swastika symbol is associated with Lakshmi, the
L603@P9: goddess of wealth, and it is used as a good luck symbol
L604@P9: to give wealth and success to the user.
L605@P9: Other geometric symbols found in the Kot Diji
L606@P9: phase occupations include drcle and dot motifS, stars
L607@P9: .nd stepped cross designs. All of these symbols can be
L608@P9: associated with cosmic order and attempts by humans
L609@P9: to give this order to their daily lives. Similar geometric seals have been found at Kot Diji Phase settlements
L610@P9: throughout the greater Indus region, and the same
L611@P9: desigos also appear on painted pottery. The implication of these repeated patterns is the emergence of a
L612@P9: repertoire of graphic symbols that appear to reflect a
L613@P9: shared set ofbeliefS. Similar widespread use ofimages of

L629@P10: one from Mound AB (Trench 39 N) and the other from
L630@P10: Mound E (NW comer, Trench 52). The stone weight
L631@P10: from Mound AB was found stratigraphically associated
L632@P10: with well-dated hearths (2800 to 2600 BeE) (Meadow
L633@P10: and Kenoyer 2005) and with indicators ofadministrative
L634@P10: control, such as geometric button seals, a day sealing
L635@P10: and a broken seal featuring an elephant. The weight was
L636@P10: made from yelloW limestone, measures 9.7 x 9.5 " 7.1
L637@P10: mm and weighs 1.7 grams. This weight belongs to the
L638@P10: 'B' category or 2nd ratio of Indus weights as defined by
L639@P10: Hemmy (Marshall 1931: 591, Table III) (see Table 9.3).
L640@P10: The second cubical stone object has slightly rounded
L641@P10: edges and one polished face and appears to have been
L642@P10: a weight that was subsequently used as a hammerstone
L643@P10: or pestle. This artefaet was made of white quartzite and
L644@P10: weighs 102.95 grams, which corresponds to the J category of Hemmy and the 160th ratio (see Table 9.3). The
L645@P10: fact that one weight was fuund within the walled ateas
L646@P10: of Mound AB, and the other within the walled area of
L647@P10: Mound E, suggests that both of the Early Harappan
L648@P10: settlement sectors at Harapp. were using the same basic
L649@P10: weight standard. This pattern continues in the later
L650@P10: Harapparr Period, when weights of the same standard
L651@P10: are found in all of the walled seetOrS of the site and at

L673@P11: .il Many scholars have speculated on the origin of the
L674@P11: Harappan weight system, and it is thought to have been
L675@P11: derived from grains (Marshall 1931), such as wheat
L676@P11: (0.048 grams) or barley (0.064 grams), or edible seeds,
L677@P11: such as mustard or mung bean (masha). One poisonous
L678@P11: seed that is widely referred to in ancient Indian texts on
L679@P11: weights is the black and red seed (gunja) ofthe wild licorice plant (Abrus precatorius) (Marshall 1931; Mainkar
L680@P11: 1984). This seed weighs between 0.109 and 0.113 grams
L681@P11: and approximately 8 seeds would correspond to the 1st
L682@P11: Indus weight ratio or 0.871 gram, as defined by Hemmy
L683@P11: (Marshall 1931). Since the actual weight of these grains
L684@P11: varies depending on where they are grown or the amount
L685@P11: of water they receive, it is difficult to determine which
L686@P11: of them was used to define the original Indus weight
L687@P11: system. Regardless ofwhat the base weight was, the system developed by the Early Harappans became widely
L688@P11: adopted during the Harappan Period.
L689@P11: Harappa Phase measurement
L690@P11: Although the basic systems of measurement needed for
L691@P11: the functioning of large towns had already been established in the Early Harappan Period, the pervasive use
L692@P11: of these systems throughout the greater Indus region
L693@P11: is only seen during the Harappan Period, from around
L694@P11: 2600 to 1900 BCE. Contrary to views taken by many
L695@P11: scholars, I do not feel that this adoption was rapid or
L696@P11: explosive, but that it happened gradually, over the course
L697@P11: of200 or 250 years, between 2600 and 2450 BCE.
L698@P11: Harappan stone weights
L699@P11: The basic weight system that evolved during the Early
L700@P11: Harappan Period became more refined and varied during the Harappan Phase. Extensive studies of weights
L701@P11: at Mohenjo-daro, Harappa and Chanhu-daro have been
L702@P11: summarized in the early excavation reports (Marshall
L703@P11: 1931; Mackay 1938, 1943), but the excavations at
L704@P11: Harappa have revealed the presence of several additional weight categories that were not reported previously (Table 9.3). Weights were used with matched scale
L705@P11: pans, which were made of copper/bronze and occasionally of terracotta. Two sets of scale pans, along with a
L706@P11: bronze cross-beam, a broken arrow-shaped pointer and
L707@P11: a hook and chain, were discovered in 1996 in the course
L708@P11: of conservation work on Mound F at Harappa (Nasir
L709@P11: 2001). The scale pans were made in two sizes; one set
L710@P11: is around 6 em in diameter with three holes for hanging the plate evenly, and the larger set is around 63 em
L711@P11: in diameter. These sizes would be appropriate for the
L712@P11: small and medium sizes of Indus weights but not the
L713@P11: largest ones.
L714@P11: The first seven Indus weights double in size from
L715@P11: 1:2:4:8:16:32:64. There are exceptions to this general
L716@P11: pattern, with some anomalous categories sllch as the
L717@P11: 8/3 ratio (approximately 2.28 grams). The most COmmon weight is the 16th ratio, which is approximately
L718@P11: 13.7 grams. At this point the weight increments change
L719@P11: to a decimal system where the next largest weights have
L720@P11: a ratio of 160, 200, 320, and 640. The next jump goes
L721@P11: to 1,600, 3,200, 6,400, 8,000, and 12,800. The largest
L722@P11: weight found at the site ofMohenjo-daro weighs 10,865
L723@P11: grams (approximately 25 pounds), which is almost
L724@P11: 100,000 times the weight of the 'gunja' seed.
L725@P11: The new categories of weights found at Harappa
L726@P11: have been designated using a modification of Hemmy's
L727@P11: system. Categories AAA, AA and A' and F' conform to
L728@P11: the earlier categories or represent slight variations (Table
L729@P11: 9.3). Categories AAA (0.3 gram) and AA (0.6 gram) are
L730@P11: quite small and they may have been missed by the earlier
L731@P11: excavators because they did not screen all of the excavation areas. Categories A' and F' may simply be anomalies.
L732@P11: A comparison ofweights from different areas ofHarappa
L733@P11: itself indicates that all of the cubical weights from the
L734@P11: entire Harappa Phase conform to one single system.
L735@P11: In addition to cubical weights, a new style of weight
L736@P11: was introduced in the latest phase of the Harappan
L737@P11: Period, Period 3C. These weights were generally made
L738@P11: from agate or chalcedony and were truncated spheres,
L739@P11: with two flat opposing surfaces to prevent them from
L740@P11: rolling away. The truncated spherical weights generally
L741@P11: conform to the same system as the cubical chert weights.
L742@P11: Their shape variation may have had some ritual or cultural significance, but they are found in all the major
L743@P11: mounds at Harappa, as well as at Mohenjo-daro (Mackay
L744@P11: 1938), Chanhu-daro (Mackay 1943), Lothal (Rao 1979)
L745@P11: and even the small site of Rojdi (Possehl and Raval
L746@P11: 1989).
L747@P11: During the Harappan Phase cubical stone weights
L748@P11: were predominantly made from a distinctive variety of
L749@P11: banded chert obtained from the Rohri hills in Sindh.
L750@P11: While some weights were made from agate, granite or
L751@P11: other patterned stones, the chert varieties are the most
L752@P11: widely distribured throughout the city and the Indus
L753@P11: region in general. Distinctive manufacturing debris for
L754@P11: cubical chert weights has been found in the agate bead
L755@P11: making areas of the site. In addition, some perfectly
L756@P11: spherical agate balls that may be unfinished weights of
L757@P11: the second type have also been found in association with
L758@P11: bead making areas. This pattern suggests that bead mak·
L759@P11: ers were also involved in the preparation of the highly
L760@P11-12: standardized weights. Measuring the Harappan world 117
L761@P12: Most scholars assume that these weights were used
L762@P12: for everyday market exchange, with the smaller weights
L763@P12: being used for precious stones and metals, perfumes and
L764@P12: valuable medicines. The larger weights are thought to
L765@P12: have been used for grain orlarge quantities ofgoods. The
L766@P12: faCt that there are relatively few weights given the size of
L767@P12: the cities and market areas suggests that this explanation
L768@P12: is probably not valid. It is much more probable that the
L769@P12: weights relate to taxation Or tithing. The recent excavations at Harappa reveal that the highest concentration
L770@P12: ofweights is located in association with gateway areas or
L771@P12: in craft production areas, where goods entering the city
L772@P12: may have been weighed and taxed. Furthermore, many
L773@P12: of the smaller sites such as Allahdino have only a single
L774@P12: set ofweights in the middle range ofvalues, while only
L775@P12: the largest sites such as Mohenjo-daro and Harappa have
L776@P12: one or two extremely large weights.
L777@P12: Some scholars have proposed a diffi:rent grouping of
L778@P12: the weights by combining all the weights from Mohenjodaro, Har.ppa, eh.nhu-daro .nd Lothal and recaleulating the averages (Mainkar 1984). This approach assumes
L779@P12: that the entire system was centrally standardized and
L780@P12: obscures the presence of regional variation. Ongoing
L781@P12: studies suggest that each major city had its own internal system ofweights that was highly standardized, with
L782@P12: general comparability to weights used in other cities, but
L783@P12: that there was a certain degree ofregional variation. More
L784@P12: precise measurements and the examination ofweights to
L785@P12: determine their condition (chipped or worn) need to be
L786@P12: undertaken to investigate this theory fully.
L787@P12: Even if the weights are not absolutely standardized
L788@P12: throughout the Indus region, there is a general standard
L789@P12: that was followed by all the Indus settlements. One of
L790@P12: the key questions that remain to be answered is who was
L791@P12: responsible for maintaining the general standardization
L792@P12: of the Indus weights over such a large area and for over
L793@P12: 700 years. This standardization could not have been
L794@P12: simply the result of a shared belief, but must have been
L795@P12: rigorously maintained by people who were most concerned with the profits or benefits of using the weights.
L796@P12: Rather than political or ideological elites, merchant communities and traders may have been the primary agents
L797@P12: in maintaining weight standardization. This interpretation is supported by the fact that the use of cubical stone
L798@P12: weights disappeared at the end of the Harappan Period,
L799@P12: but the actual system of weights continued to be used
L800@P12: during the Early Historical Period and is still used today
L801@P12: throughout South Asia (MarshaBlnl; Mainkar 1984).
L802@P12: Other artefacts associated with Indus political au thority
L803@P12: as well as trade and ideologies are inscribed seals, many
L804@P12: of which included animal symbols such as the 'unicorn'
L805@P12: or other totemic animals. At ti,e end of the Indus cities,

L810@P12: Harappan linear measurements and brick sizes
L811@P12: On the basis of two rare discoveries of what have been
L812@P12: referred to as scales, combined with careful analysis of
L813@P12: architectural thtures, the earlier excavators calculated
L814@P12: that there were two systems of linear measnrement at
L815@P12: usc in the Indus cities, the foot (13.2 inches or 33.35
L816@P12: em) and the cubit (20.8 inches or 52.83 cm) (Marshall
L817@P12: 1931; Mackay 1938; Vats 1940). A fragmentary bonze
L818@P12: rod (1.5 inches long) with incised lines found at Harappa
L819@P12: is thought to have been a measuring tool, with four divisions that average 0.37 inch or 0.93 em (Vats 1940: 365­
L820@P12: 366). An incised shell plaque from Mohenjo-daro had five
L821@P12: divisions of 1.32 inches or 3.35 em (Mackay. 1938: 404- .
L822@P12: 405). These measuring devices made of bronze and shell
L823@P12: may have been prepared for some special occasion or elite
L824@P12: consumer, but the average person living in these dties
L825@P12: probably used other means ofmeasurement.
L826@P12-13: One of the most common measurements in traditional South Asian culture is the width ofthe hand (four 118 J. Mark Kenoyer
L827@P13: finger widths or angula- approximately 7 to 9 cm). Other
L828@P13: measurements include various types of hand spans, the
L829@P13: distance from the elbow to the tip of the finger (cubit),
L830@P13: the foot, two feet, a pace, the distance between the tips
L831@P13: il of the fingers of both outstretched arms and the vertical
L832@P13: distance from the feet to the tip of the hands stretched
L833@P13: above the head. The hand measurement is perhaps the
L834@P13: most relevant for understanding Harappan architecture,
L835@P13: because it is basically the same as the thickness of a wet
L836@P13: mud brick.
L837@P13: Experiments with mud brick manufacture show that
L838@P13: the wet clay shrinks around 0.5 em in thickness and
L839@P13: width and up to 2 cm in overall length. If a mud brick
L840@P13: is made with the width of the hand for thickness, and
L841@P13: double that for width, and double that for length, one
L842@P13: ends up with a brick that measures 8 x 16 x 32 cm. After
L843@P13: drying, the brick will measure 7.5 x 15.5 x 30 cm, and
L844@P13: when a brick is fired there is even more shrinkage. This
L845@P13: system of measurement is the most likely explanation
L846@P13: for the standardized brick shapes, and the proportions
